lessons.title: Describing your experience
lessons.goal: Talk about your job, your tasks and your experience.

tip.title: seit + present tense
tip.body: For something that started in the past and still continues, German uses the present tense with seit: Ich arbeite seit drei Jahren als Projektmanager. Finished experience uses the Perfekt: Vorher habe ich bei einer kleinen Firma gearbeitet. Professional tip: speak a little slower than usual and finish your sentences clearly; it sounds confident.

lessons.title: The job interview
lessons.goal: Answer typical interview questions and ask your own questions politely.

tip.title: Indirect questions
tip.body: Polite questions are often indirect: Können Sie mir sagen, wie das Team aussieht? Ich würde gern wissen, ob man im Homeoffice arbeiten kann. After the question word or ob, the verb goes to the end. Interview tip: "Das ist eine gute Frage" is a perfectly natural way to win a few seconds before you answer.

lessons.title: The application
lessons.goal: Talk about applying for a job, using wegen and während.

tip.title: Genitive after wegen and während
tip.body: In formal German, wegen (because of) and während (during) take the genitive: wegen des Umzugs, während des Studiums, wegen der Arbeit. Masculine and neuter nouns add -s or -es. In casual speech you will hear wegen dem Umzug, but in an interview or a letter the genitive sounds more polished.

lessons.title: Relative clauses and indirect questions
lessons.goal: Describe jobs and people precisely and ask questions politely.

tip.title: Two kinds of verb-final clauses
tip.body: A relative pronoun takes the gender of its noun and the case of its role in the clause: eine Stelle, die …; der Kollege, mit dem ich arbeite. An indirect question starts with ob (yes/no) or a question word after a polite opener like Können Sie mir sagen …? In both, the conjugated verb goes to the end.

lessons.title: The job interview in Vienna
lessons.goal: Present yourself well — how you come across decides the outcome.

culture.title: Frau Magister, Herr Doktor
culture.body: In Austria, academic titles are part of polite address: Frau Magister Gruber, Herr Doktor Huber, even Herr Diplomingenieur. Using the title in a formal setting is a sign of respect. In Germany, Dr. is mainly used in letters and for medical doctors (Frau Doktor), and in Switzerland titles are rarely used when speaking.

lessons.title: Introduce yourself in an interview

culture.title: The German Bewerbung
culture.body: A typical application includes a cover letter (Anschreiben), a tabular CV (Lebenslauf) and copies of certificates and references (Zeugnisse). A professional photo on the CV is still common in Germany, Austria and Switzerland, though it is optional. Employer references (Arbeitszeugnisse) use a coded polite language, so "stets zu unserer vollsten Zufriedenheit" means top marks.
